lessons.title: Saying it more precisely

words.meaning: A very small difference in meaning.
words.example: The nuance is lost in translation.

words.meaning: It can be argued that.
words.example: This is arguably the best option.

words.meaning: Very small and barely important.
words.example: The difference was marginal.

words.meaning: Convincing and hard to argue with.
words.example: She made a compelling case.

words.meaning: To think something is smaller than it is.
words.example: Do not underestimate the cost.

listen: The improvement was real but marginal, and arguably not worth the disruption.
What makes the argument compelling is not the data but the framing.
speak: The difference is marginal rather than decisive.
This is arguably the strongest option we have.

grammar.title: Hedging and softening
grammar.rule: Advanced speakers rarely state things absolutely: they qualify claims.
examples: It tends to work better in practice.
This may well be the deciding factor.
There is a case for waiting.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence hedges the claim?
options: This is arguably the best option.
quiz.explanation: Arguably marks it as an argument, not a fact.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The effect was ___ rather than dramatic.
quiz.explanation: Marginal contrasts with dramatic.

quiz.prompt: Which is the most cautious?
quiz.explanation: Might expresses possibility.

lessons.title: Idiomatic English

words.meaning: To do something badly to save time.
words.example: They cut corners on testing.

words.meaning: In agreement.
words.example: Let us make sure we are on the same page.

words.meaning: To accept something unpleasant.
words.example: We bit the bullet and rewrote it.

words.meaning: Unlikely to succeed.
words.example: It is a long shot, but worth trying.

words.meaning: To decide as you go.
words.example: Let us play it by ear.

listen: We could not agree on a date, so we decided to play it by ear.
It is a long shot, but if it works we save a month.
speak: I want to make sure we are on the same page.
We had to bite the bullet and start again.

grammar.title: Idioms and collocation
grammar.rule: Idioms are fixed: changing one word breaks them. Learn the whole phrase.
examples: Correct: cut corners. Wrong: cut the corners.
Correct: make a decision. Wrong: do a decision.
Correct: take a risk. Wrong: make a risk.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct collocation.
quiz.explanation: Make collocates with decision.

quiz.prompt: It is a long shot means it is:
Choose the correct idiom.
quiz.explanation: Idioms are fixed phrases.

lessons.title: Formal presentations

words.meaning: To give the main points.
words.example: Let me outline the plan.

words.meaning: To draw attention to something.
words.example: I want to highlight two risks.

words.meaning: A likely result of something.
words.example: The implication is a longer timeline.

words.meaning: The most important fact.
words.example: The bottom line is cost.

words.meaning: To give a short final summary.
words.example: To sum up, we recommend option B.

listen: Let me outline three points, then I will take questions at the end.
To sum up: the cost is higher, but the risk is significantly lower.
speak: Let me outline the three main points.
To sum up, I recommend the second option.

grammar.title: Signposting language
grammar.rule: Signposts tell the listener where you are, which is what makes a talk easy to follow.
examples: First, I will cover the background.
Moving on to the second point.
That brings me to my conclusion.

quiz.prompt: Which phrase signals a summary?
quiz.explanation: To sum up closes a talk.

quiz.prompt: Complete: That ___ me to my final point.
quiz.explanation: Brings me to is the fixed phrase.

quiz.prompt: Which word means a likely result?

lessons.title: Building an argument

words.meaning: Facts that support a claim.
words.example: The evidence points the other way.

words.meaning: An argument against yours.
words.example: Let me address the counterargument.

words.meaning: To weaken something gradually.
words.example: That figure undermines the whole case.

words.meaning: The idea an argument starts from.
words.example: The premise is questionable.

words.meaning: To admit a point is true.
words.example: I concede that the cost is high.

listen: I concede the first point, but the evidence for the second is much weaker.
The strongest counterargument is cost, so let me address it directly.
speak: I concede that point, but it does not change the conclusion.
The evidence for that claim is thin.

grammar.title: Concession structures
grammar.rule: Granting a point before answering it makes an argument far more persuasive.
examples: While I accept the cost, the risk is lower.
Granted, it is slower. It is also safer.
Even if that is true, it does not follow that we should stop.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence concedes then counters?
options: While it is expensive, it lasts twice as long.
quiz.explanation: Concession plus counter is the persuasive shape.

quiz.prompt: Complete: Even ___ that is true, the conclusion does not follow.
quiz.explanation: Even if introduces a hypothetical concession.

quiz.prompt: Which word means to weaken gradually?

lessons.title: Negotiating

words.meaning: Power that helps you get what you want.
words.example: We have very little leverage here.

words.meaning: An agreement where both sides give something.
words.example: We reached a compromise.

words.meaning: Able to change.
words.example: We can be flexible on timing.

words.meaning: To leave a negotiation.
words.example: We are prepared to walk away.

words.meaning: A condition you cannot accept.
words.example: The delivery date is a deal breaker.

listen: We can be flexible on the timeline, but the budget is a deal breaker.
If we cannot agree on support, we are prepared to walk away.
speak: We can be flexible on timing if you can move on price.
That would be a deal breaker for us.

grammar.title: Conditional bargaining
grammar.rule: Trade concessions with if clauses so nothing is given away for free.
examples: If you can move on price, we can be flexible on delivery.
We would consider that, provided the support is included.
Were you to extend the contract, we could reduce the rate.

quiz.prompt: Which is a conditional trade?
options: If you extend the contract, we can reduce the rate.
quiz.explanation: The concession is tied to a condition.

quiz.prompt: Complete: We would agree, ___ support is included.
quiz.explanation: Provided introduces a condition.

quiz.prompt: A deal breaker is something you:

lessons.title: Difficult conversations

words.meaning: To deal with a problem directly.
words.example: We need to address the delay.

words.meaning: Reacting as if attacked.
words.example: He became defensive immediately.

words.meaning: To accept that something is true.
words.example: I acknowledge the frustration.

words.meaning: To make bigger, or to take to a manager.
words.example: Let us not escalate this.

words.meaning: Something both sides agree on.
words.example: Let us start from common ground.

listen: I want to acknowledge that the last month has been difficult before we talk about next steps.
Rather than escalate, can we find some common ground first?
speak: I want to acknowledge how difficult this has been.
Can we start from what we agree on?

grammar.title: Depersonalising language
grammar.rule: Describing the situation instead of blaming the person keeps the conversation open.
examples: Blaming: You missed the deadline.
Neutral: The deadline was missed and I want to understand why.
Neutral: There seems to be a gap between what we expected.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is least likely to trigger defensiveness?
options: There seems to be a gap in expectations.
quiz.explanation: It describes the situation, not the person.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I want to ___ that this has been hard.
quiz.explanation: Acknowledge accepts the other side feeling.

quiz.prompt: Common ground means:

lessons.title: Claims and evidence

words.meaning: A confident statement made without proof.
words.example: That is an assertion, not a finding.

words.meaning: To confirm with independent support.
words.example: Two other studies corroborate it.

words.meaning: Based on personal stories rather than data.
words.example: The evidence is purely anecdotal.

words.meaning: Strong enough to survive scrutiny.
words.example: The finding is robust across samples.

words.meaning: To wrongly treat two things as one.
words.example: The article conflates cost and value.

listen: My objection is not that the claim is false. It is that nothing in the paper corroborates it.
We keep conflating two questions here, and until we separate them we will talk past each other.
speak: The evidence is largely anecdotal.
I think we are conflating two separate questions.

grammar.title: Distancing yourself from a claim
grammar.rule: It is claimed that, the argument goes and on this account report a position without adopting it.
examples: It is claimed that the policy worked.
The argument goes that prices would fall.
On this account, the delay was unavoidable.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence reports a claim without endorsing it?
options: It is claimed that the policy worked.
quiz.explanation: It is claimed that distances the speaker.

quiz.prompt: Which word means to wrongly treat two things as one?
quiz.explanation: Conflate means to merge wrongly.

quiz.prompt: Evidence based only on personal stories is ___.

lessons.title: Cause, correlation and consequence

words.meaning: To say something was caused by a particular thing.
words.example: They attribute the fall to the weather.

words.meaning: To happen at the same time.
words.example: The two changes coincided exactly.

words.meaning: Hidden beneath the visible surface.
words.example: The underlying cause was never addressed.

words.meaning: A result that then causes further results.
words.example: The strike had a knock-on effect on deliveries.

words.meaning: Appearing genuine but actually false.
words.example: That is a spurious correlation.

listen: The two trends coincide, certainly. Coinciding is not the same as causing, and the paper knows that.
Fixing the symptom without touching the underlying cause bought us about six weeks.
speak: The two things coincide, but I would not attribute one to the other.
The underlying cause is different from the one being reported.

grammar.title: Cause and effect linkers
grammar.rule: Because and since introduce a cause; consequently, hence and as a result introduce an effect.
examples: Since demand fell, we cut the order.
Demand fell; consequently, we cut the order.
Hence the revision.

quiz.prompt: Which linker introduces a consequence?
quiz.explanation: Consequently marks a result.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The data ___ with the policy change, but proves nothing on its own.
quiz.explanation: Coincide means happen at the same time.

quiz.prompt: A relationship that looks real but is not is ___.

lessons.title: Conceding and rebutting

words.meaning: Used to admit a point before disagreeing.
words.example: Granted, the cost is high.

words.meaning: Despite.
words.example: Notwithstanding the delay, it worked.

words.meaning: To describe as more important than it is.
words.example: I think you overstate the risk.

words.meaning: A condition attached to an agreement.
words.example: I accept, with one proviso about the timing.

words.meaning: To add a limit to a statement.
words.example: Let me qualify that slightly.

listen: Granted, the first year was expensive. Notwithstanding that, the running cost is now lower than before.
I take the principle. What I would qualify is the scale you are claiming for it.
speak: Granted, the cost was higher than planned.
I take that point, but I would add one proviso.

grammar.title: Concession structures
grammar.rule: While, whereas and much as concede a point inside the same sentence as the rebuttal.
examples: While I accept the cost, the benefit is larger.
Much as I agree in principle, the timing is wrong.
Whereas the first study was small, the second was not.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ I agree in principle, the timing is wrong.
quiz.explanation: Much as concedes a point.

quiz.prompt: Which word means to add a limit to a statement?
quiz.explanation: Qualify narrows a claim.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ the delay, the project came in under budget.
quiz.explanation: Notwithstanding means despite.

lessons.title: Matching the register

words.meaning: Following official or serious convention.
words.example: The formal version goes to the board.

words.meaning: Belonging to ordinary conversation.
words.example: That phrasing is too colloquial for a report.

words.meaning: Using far more words than necessary.
words.example: The draft is accurate but verbose.

words.meaning: Expressed clearly in few words.
words.example: Keep the summary succinct.

words.meaning: The attitude a piece of writing conveys.
words.example: The tone reads as annoyed.

listen: It is not wrong, it is just verbose. Cut it by half and the argument gets stronger, not weaker.
The tone is the problem rather than the content. It reads as annoyed, and I do not think you are.
speak: The draft is accurate but far too verbose.
I would make the summary more succinct.

grammar.title: Nominalisation and formality
grammar.rule: Formal English turns verbs into nouns: we decided becomes the decision was taken. It is more distant, and often less clear.
examples: We decided to delay. -> The decision was taken to delay.
They failed to reply. -> There was no response.
We will investigate. -> An investigation will follow.

quiz.prompt: Which is the more formal version?
options: The decision was taken to stop.
quiz.explanation: Nominalisation raises formality.

quiz.prompt: Which word means expressed clearly in few words?
A phrase that belongs in conversation but not a report is ___.

lessons.title: Difficult messages

words.meaning: Honest even when it is uncomfortable.
words.example: Let me be candid about the timeline.

words.meaning: The amount by which something is less than needed.
words.example: There is a shortfall of two weeks.

words.meaning: To make something bad less severe.
words.example: We can mitigate the delay by resequencing.

words.meaning: Responsible and required to explain.
words.example: I am accountable for this decision.

words.meaning: A plan for something that might go wrong.
words.example: We built in a two-week contingency.

listen: I want to be candid: there is a two-week shortfall and no contingency left to absorb it.
I am accountable for the estimate. What I can offer now is a way to mitigate it, not to undo it.
speak: I want to be candid about where we are.
I am accountable for that estimate.

grammar.title: Taking responsibility without hedging it away
grammar.rule: The active voice names the actor. In bad news, the passive can read as evasion.
examples: I underestimated the work. (owns it)
The work was underestimated. (hides who)
We will fix it by Friday. (commits)

quiz.prompt: Which sentence takes responsibility most clearly?
options: It turned out to be wrong.
quiz.explanation: The active voice names the actor.

quiz.prompt: Which word means to make something bad less severe?
A plan for something that might go wrong is a ___.

lessons.title: Speaking with impact

words.meaning: Special importance given to something.
words.example: Put the emphasis on the second point.

words.meaning: A short silence used deliberately.
words.example: A pause there does more than a louder voice.

words.meaning: A sound or word used while thinking.
words.example: Cut the fillers and you sound certain.

words.meaning: The speed at which you speak.
words.example: Slow the pace for the key sentence.

words.meaning: Able to convince someone.
words.example: That is a persuasive argument.

listen: You do not need a louder voice. You need a pause before the number, so it has somewhere to land.
The content was persuasive. The pace was not - the whole middle went past too fast to follow.
speak: I want to put the emphasis on the second point.
That is a persuasive argument, and here is my one reservation.

grammar.title: Fronting for emphasis
grammar.rule: Move the important element to the front of the sentence. It changes the emphasis without changing the meaning.
examples: That, I disagree with.
What worries me is the timeline.
Never before had we missed a date.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence emphasises the timeline?
options: What worries me is the timeline.
quiz.explanation: The cleft moves it into focus.

quiz.prompt: Which word means the speed at which you speak?
Complete: Never before ___ we faced this.
quiz.explanation: Fronting a negative triggers inversion.
